title: Respiratory protection and fit: the last layer of control
audience: Timber floor restoration workers who may need respiratory protection, and supervisors who select and record it.
learningOutcomes: Explain why respiratory protection is the last layer of control, after extraction and other measures.
Select a respirator and filter type from the assessment and its markings, and state the standards named by the regulators.
Carry out a fit check before every use of a facial-seal respirator, and record it.
referencesAtStart: Official sources for this lesson: WorkSafe Victoria, Wood dust: health hazards and control (reviewed 17 April 2026); NSW Government, LeadSmart: renovating and maintenance (published 18 May 2026; last modified 20 July 2026).

instruction.heading: Respirators are the last layer
instruction.body: WorkSafe Victoria (reviewed 17/04/2026) says a respirator is needed where the higher controls cannot hold exposure within the limits. A respirator protects only the person wearing it, and it works only when it fits and is the right type. It is not a substitute for extraction, damp cleaning or isolation of the work area. If the controls are not set up, the job does not start until they are.

instruction.heading: Choosing the respirator and filter
instruction.body: For wood dust, WorkSafe Victoria (reviewed 17/04/2026) indicates that a non-disposable half-face unit fitted with a P2 filter generally meets the need. The same page points to AS/NZS 1715 for selection guidance, cites AS/NZS 1716:2012 as the marking to look for, and names a powered air purifying respirator (PAPR) as an alternative. For old paint, NSW LeadSmart (published 18 May 2026) advises an AS 1716-approved respirator or a P1 or P2 mask with coveralls, and says paper masks often fit poorly and do not block fine dust.

instruction.heading: Fit, facial hair and fit testing
instruction.body: Facial-seal respirators need clean-shaven users and a fit check every time they are put on. The WorkSafe Victoria page (reviewed 17/04/2026) says a fit test should be carried out, using either the quantitative or the qualitative method. A person with facial hair that breaks the seal cannot be fit checked on a facial-seal respirator, so the assessment must select a different option, such as a PAPR, before the work proceeds.

instruction.heading: Care, storage and records
instruction.body: Clean and store the respirator after each use, outside the work area. Keep a record of each respirator issued, its fit test, and the training given. A respirator that is damaged, has a poor seal, or breathes poorly is taken out of use.

procedure: Confirm the exposure assessment that calls for respiratory protection, and the controls already in place.
Select the respirator and filter type from the assessment, and check the markings against AS/NZS 1716 or an equivalent.
For a facial-seal respirator, confirm the user is clean-shaven and complete a fit check before every use.
Put on eye protection, coveralls and gloves where the assessment requires them.
Remove and clean the respirator outside the work area, and wash hands and face.
Record the respirator issued, the fit test and the training, and report any damage or poor fit.

workedExamples.situation: A worker with a full beard is assigned a half-face respirator with a P2 filter for a sanding job. The worker says the respirator 'will be fine'.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is the correct action before the work starts?
workedExamples.reasoning: A facial-seal respirator needs a clean-shaven user and a fit check each time it is worn. A bearded worker cannot be fit checked on that type. The assessment must select an option such as a PAPR, or the worker must not start the task until a suitable option is arranged and recorded. The worker does not use a paper mask as a substitute.

equipmentAndPpe: Half-face, non-disposable respirator with a P2 filter, or an equivalent selected by the assessment
PAPR where the assessment selects it
Coveralls, eye protection and gloves as the assessment requires

commonErrors.error: Using a paper dust mask for fine wood dust or lead dust.
commonErrors.prevention: Use a respirator selected under AS/NZS 1715 and the assessment.

commonErrors.error: Wearing a facial-seal respirator with a beard.
commonErrors.prevention: Select a different option, such as a PAPR, and do not start until it is in place.

commonErrors.error: Relying on a respirator when extraction has not been set up.
commonErrors.prevention: Set up the higher controls first, then confirm the need for a respirator.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: WorkSafe Victoria (page reviewed 17/04/2026) says a respirator is needed where higher controls cannot hold exposure within the limits, and that a non-disposable half-face unit with a P2 filter generally meets the wood dust need.

NSW LeadSmart (published 18 May 2026) advises an AS 1716-approved respirator or a P1 or P2 mask with coveralls for stripping or sanding lead paint, and says paper masks may not protect against fine dust.
Completing this lesson does not authorise anyone to carry out lead-related work or fit testing unless the program and the law allow it.

qualityStandard: The respirator is selected from the assessment and its markings meet AS/NZS 1716 or an equivalent.
A fit check is completed and recorded before every use of a facial-seal respirator.
No task requiring respiratory protection starts without a suitable, fit-checked respirator.
documentationEvidence: Respirator issue and fit test record
Training record for the respirator program
summary: Respirators are the last layer, after extraction, cleaning and isolation.
A facial-seal respirator needs a clean-shaven user and a fit check every time.
Paper masks are not the protection for fine dust or lead dust.
referencesAtEnd: Official sources to recheck before any job: WorkSafe Victoria, Wood dust: health hazards and control (reviewed 17 April 2026); NSW Government, LeadSmart: renovating and maintenance (published 18 May 2026; last modified 20 July 2026).

knowledgeChecks.question: What is WorkSafe Victoria's position on respiratory protection?
options: It is the first control to use on every job site and in every room at the start
It is needed only where higher controls do not keep exposure within the standards
It replaces extraction on every sander, tool, vacuum and dust bag on the site
It is not needed at all on any timber job, floor or sanding task today

knowledgeChecks.question: Which filter does WorkSafe Victoria say is usually sufficient for a half-face respirator for wood dust?
options: No
P1
P2
AX

knowledgeChecks.question: Why must a facial-seal respirator be fit checked each time it is put on?
options: To change its colour on the face
To extend the life of the filter
It is not required on the job at all
To confirm a good seal against the face

knowledgeChecks.question: A worker has a full beard. What is the correct action for a facial-seal respirator?
options: Trim the beard, or use a PAPR or another option selected by the assessment
Wear it anyway, since it will still seal well enough for the whole job today
Remove the respirator and sand the surface without any cover
Use a paper mask instead of the respirator on the site today

knowledgeChecks.question: What does NSW LeadSmart say about paper masks when stripping or sanding lead paint?
options: They are fully protective
They may not protect against fine dust
They are preferred by regulators
They are required by law in every state
